prerequisites: Compares and distinguishes related concepts and their properties from basic computer science and/or mathematics disciplines.

learning_outcomes.text: Defines fundamental concepts from basic mathematics disciplines.
Compares and distinguishes related notions and their properties from basic mathematics disciplines.
Formulates observations, differentiates notions, properties, and assertions from basic mathematics disciplines through examples and counterexamples.
Defines basic concepts from advanced mathematics disciplines in the curriculum.
Compares and distinguishes related notions and their properties from advanced mathematics disciplines in the curriculum.
Formulates observations, differentiates notions, properties, and assertions from advanced mathematics disciplines through examples and counterexamples.
Defines concepts from basic computer science and/or applied mathematics disciplines.
Compares and distinguishes related notions and their properties from basic computer science and/or applied mathematics disciplines.
Formulates observations and differentiates notions, properties, and assertions from basic computer science and/or applied mathematics disciplines through examples and counterexamples.
Indicates and recognizes the concepts involved in the requirements of exercises and problems formulated in the disciplines of the curriculum.
Provides examples of using basic theoretical concepts and results to solve exercises and problems formulated in connection with the topics covered in the curriculum disciplines.
Recognizes and analyzes the necessary and/or sufficient conditions in the statement of mathematical assertions and specifies their role in the proof.
Identifies and describes the essential elements in the construction of proofs of mathematical assertions (lemmas, propositions, theorems), recognizes reasoning errors, and corrects them.
Answers questions and correctly and rigorously formulates the statements of mathematical assertions (lemmas, propositions, theorems) from the curriculum disciplines.
Reproduces, analyzes hypotheses and conclusions from mathematical assertions, and discusses how they can be linked in the proof.

Argues the role of elements in the hypothesis of mathematical assertions, discusses how they are articulated in the proof, and independently constructs correct proofs of mathematical assertions within major mathematics disciplines.
Identifies and applies appropriate techniques for solving exercises and problems in major mathematics disciplines.
Identifies and applies appropriate techniques for solving problems in advanced mathematics disciplines.
Describes real-world problems in mathematical terms, identifies working hypotheses, constructs appropriate mathematical models, and explains the limitations of the models thus obtained.
Uses numerical methods and software packages to solve constructed mathematical models and interprets the mathematical results obtained from the perspective of the modeled practical problem.

Uses logical thinking, analyzes problem statements, selects the specific method for solving them, and uses logical schemes and work diagrams in solving problems from the topics covered in the curriculum disciplines.

Adapts routine problem-solving techniques and strategies to solve synthesis problems with a higher degree of complexity and uses various representations to illustrate or justify problem-solving methods.
Realizes particularizations or generalizations, starting from a given property or problem, and independently writes complete solutions to problems solved in the covered topics.

Extends common problem-solving techniques to problems that arise in new situations with progressively increasing difficulty, seeks other solving methods, and formulates consequences and conclusions that follow from a set of hypotheses.

Analyzes solving methods, establishes the uniqueness of solutions, recognizes reasoning errors in solving a problem, finds ways to eliminate them, and obtains the correct version of the proof/solving method.

Verifies, in particular cases or by constructing examples or counterexamples, the validity of mathematical statements. The student/graduate translates a practical situation into mathematical language, solves the obtained problem, and interprets the obtained results.
Identifies and correlates connections between seemingly unrelated concepts from major mathematics disciplines.

Summarizes, classifies, and presents the conclusions of given problems using various types of representations and communicates mathematical concepts and reasoning clearly and efficiently to specialists and non-specialists through written reports and oral presentations.

Solves problems using analytical and/or numerical methods and uses dedicated software packages or writes elaborate codes to solve practical problems and mathematical models constructed using partial differential equations or other tools from the covered curriculum.

Uses independent information and documentation methods, which offer an opening to continuous learning, elaborates scientific communications or reports, and makes complete bibliographical references by observing ethical norms when citing documentation sources used. The student/graduate approaches problem-solving from different angles and directions, including based on non-traditional methodologies, to use them in computer science for other applications of mathematics.

syllabus_topics: Elements of error theory and floating-point arithmetic
Elements of error theory and floating-point arithmetic. Systems of linear equations. Frobenius matrices and solving systems by Gauss method
Systems with symmetric and positive definite matrices; Cholesky method.
(Arbitrary) systems of linear equations. Orthogonal matrices, Douse Q)lder method
Matrix norms. Iterative methods for solving systems of linear equations
Iterative methods for solving systems of linear equations. Relaxation methods
Conjugate gradient method. Least squares method
Systems of nonlinear equations. Successive approximation method
Nonlinear equations and systems of equations. Newton-Raphson method
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Function interpolation. Lagrange interpolation polynomial
Function interpolation. Interpolation by spline functions
Numerical integration
Numerical solution of the Cauchy problem for differential equations - single-step methods
Numerical solution of the Cauchy problem for differential equations - multi-step methods

Brief presentation of the MATLAB program; solving introductory problems. Solving systems of linear equations by Gauss' method. Application: determining a conic passing through five points and not containing the origin.

Solving systems of linear equations with symmetric and positive definite system matrix by Cholesky method. Householder method for solving systems of linear equations. Application: determining a quadric passing through nine points and not containing the origin.

Iterative methods for solving systems of linear equations: Jacobi method and Gauss-Seidel method. Relaxation methods: simple relaxation, conjugate gradients. Application: temperature distribution in a material plate knowing the boundary temperature.
Solving nonlinear systems by successive approximation method or Newton-Raphson method. Application: determining extreme points for a function of several variables.
Function interpolation using Lagrange interpolation polynomial or cubic spline functions. Application: determining the trajectory of a material point knowing intermediate points.

Numerical integration. Trapezoidal formula, Simpson's formula. Application: determining the length of a material wire, mass, center of gravity, and mechanical work done by a force on the material wire.
Numerical solution of the Cauchy problem using Taylor's method or Runge-Kutta type methods. Application: studying the current in an RLC circuit or the concentration of a substance in a reservoir.
teaching_methods: Learning by discovery models (experiment, demonstration, modeling)
assessment_rules: The final evaluation result for a discipline is obtained by considering the scores and weights allocated to each activity within the discipline. Integer grades from 1 to 10 will be awarded, with a grade of 5 certifying the acquisition of the minimum learning outcomes for a discipline and the granting of its associated study credits.
